Cloud Mac for game studios: iOS and macOS builds, tests, releases

Reviewed: 2026-11-21 · WodeMac

Engines such as Unity and Unreal let you develop on Windows, but the final compile, signing and packaging of iOS and macOS builds happen in Xcode on macOS. A game team without a spare Mac can use a dedicated cloud Mac that stays online 24/7 as its build machine: pull the code, export or receive the Xcode project, build and sign, run simulator tests and upload to App Store Connect. The Apple developer account and signing certificates stay with your team.

Why iOS builds need a Mac

Xcode runs only on macOS, and compiling, signing and submitting iOS, iPadOS and macOS apps all go through the Xcode toolchain. You can do most engine work on Windows, but producing the iOS build still takes a Mac. Apple's macOS license allows macOS only on Apple-branded hardware, so a generic cloud server is not a substitute.

WodeMac rents physical M6 Mac minis (12-core CPU, 16GB unified memory, 256GB storage) in California, each to one customer, with admin rights so you can install Xcode, Git, Homebrew and the engine version you need.

The cloud Mac as a build machine

  1. Install Xcode and its command line tools; if you export the project on the Mac, install the same engine version the project uses.
  2. Pull the branch or tag you are releasing from your Git repository.
  3. Export the Xcode project with the engine's command-line or batch mode (see the engine's documentation for options), or receive a project exported on Windows.
  4. Archive and export the app with xcodebuild.
  5. Upload through App Store Connect and distribute to testers with TestFlight, using your team's own Apple Developer Program membership.
  6. Copy logs and build output to team storage, then free up space on the Mac.
xcodebuild -project YourGame.xcodeproj -scheme YourGame \
  -configuration Release -archivePath build/YourGame.xcarchive archive
xcodebuild -exportArchive -archivePath build/YourGame.xcarchive \
  -exportOptionsPlist ExportOptions.plist -exportPath build/export

Testing and nightly builds

List available simulators with xcrun simctl list devices and run tests on them with xcodebuild test. Nightly builds can run on a launchd schedule, or you can add the Mac to the continuous integration system your team already uses as a macOS build node, for example by installing Jenkins, GitLab Runner or a self-hosted GitHub Actions runner yourself.

The Mac sits in a data center in California, so you cannot plug your test phones into it. Device testing usually goes through TestFlight: team members install the build on their own devices and report back.

Storage, memory and permitted use

  • 256GB is not generous for a large game project: check out only the branch you are building, manage large assets with Git LFS, and clear DerivedData, old archives and old builds regularly.
  • 16GB of memory suits one full build at a time; watch memory pressure before running several builds together.
  • Use is limited to software development and testing: building, testing and packaging. Under the WodeMac terms and Apple's macOS license it is not a render farm or a host for unrelated batch work.
  • WodeMac and the hosting provider keep admin access for maintenance, so plan how you store signing certificates and keys.

FAQ

Can a Unity project developed on Windows be built for iOS on a cloud Mac?

Yes. Export the Xcode project on Windows and move it to the cloud Mac, or install the same engine version on the Mac and export there, then build, sign and upload with Xcode. Export options are in the engine's documentation.

Can we connect our test phones to the Mac?

No. The Mac is in a data center in California and cannot reach devices in your office. Test on simulators on the Mac and distribute device builds to your team through TestFlight.

Who provides the developer account and signing certificates?

Your team holds and manages them. WodeMac provides the machine only and does not open Apple developer accounts or supply certificates.

Is 256GB of storage enough?

It depends on the size of your project and assets. Check out only what you need, use Git LFS for large files and clean build output regularly; run one full build of your real project to confirm.
